title: profiling-tooling-and-scripts-runbook-v4
body:
Purpose
This runbook describes the profiling tooling, scripts, and CI jobs we use to investigate serving-runtime performance regressions. It is intended for engineers debugging latency/throughput issues and for owning perf CI artifacts. Contains: triage flow, commands to collect flamegraphs and traces, perf CI job templates, common bottlenecks, and preservation/retention guidance.

When to use
- New latency regressions observed in synthetic or production traffic.
- Throughput drop after model or runtime change.
- Spikes in p95/p99 token latency or CPU/GPU utilization anomalies.
- Investigating tail latency increases or increased retry rates.

Quick triage flow (high level)
1) Reproduce: Run the same workload locally or in a staging cluster (model + input shape + batch config). Use the synthetic driver with real prompt sets when possible.
2) Baseline: Confirm regression vs a known-good commit (use perf-ci artifacts or a pinned bench). If not reproducible, collect traces from production sampling.
3) Collect artifacts: CPU flamegraph, Java/Go/Rust profiler snapshot as applicable, GPU traces (nsight/cupti) if GPU-bound, kernel/perf data, and application logs.
4) Analyze: Look for hotspots (syscalls, scheduling, memcpy, kernel stalls, model kernel fallback). Compare to baseline flamegraphs.
5) Mitigate: Apply short-term mitigations (rate-limit, fallback model variant, reduce batch size) and file an engineering follow-up.

Environment and conventions
- Artifact naming: <service>-<test>-<commit>-<timestamp> (e.g., runtime-e2e-batch32-0a1b2c3-20260220T1530Z).
- Storage: S3 perf-artifacts/<service>/<yyyy-mm>/<artifact>. Keep metadata JSON adjacent.
- Retention: CI artifacts kept 90 days by default; production-sampled traces kept 180 days unless tagged for long-term study.
- CI job names: perf/baseline, perf/regression, perf/bench.<name>.
- Use docker images tagged with commit SHA for repeatable profiling.

Required tools (hosted on internal images)
- Linux perf (perf) and perf script
- Brendan Gregg FlameGraph scripts (flamegraph.pl, stackcollapse-perf.pl)
- async-profiler (for JVM-based components)
- pprof (Go/Rust builds with pprof enabled)
- Linux bpftrace / eBPF (bcc) for I/O and syscall hotspots
- nvprof / Nsight Systems or CUPTI-based trace collector for GPU
- speedscope and speedscope-cli for interactive flame/timeline view
- jaeger/zipkin tracing for distributed request traces

Collecting CPU flamegraphs (native services)
1) Ensure the service is built with frame pointers or enable unwinding flags.
2) Start workload (synthetic or mirrored traffic). Warm up for 30–120s to reach steady state.
3) Run perf: sudo perf record -F 99 -a -g -- sleep 60 (adjust duration).
4) Convert: sudo perf script | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded
5) Generate flamegraph: ./flamegraph.pl out.folded > flame-<id>.svg
6) Save metadata: git commit, docker image, workload parameters, and node specs.
7) Upload to S3 and link in the Jira ticket.

Collecting async-profiler (JVM)
- Use the bundled async-profiler in the debug image. Example: ./profiler.sh -d 60 -f /tmp/profile.svg <pid>. Options: -e cpu, alloc, lock. Use flamegraph and collapsed stacks for comparison.

Collecting pprof (Go/Rust)
- Enable pprof endpoint (default /debug/pprof or runtime/pprof).
- Collect CPU profile: curl -s localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=60 > cpu.prof
- Generate svg: go tool pprof -svg ./bin/service cpu.prof > cpu.svg or use 'pprof -http' for interactive.

GPU traces
- Nsight Systems exports timeline; use for kernel launch timing and memcpy. For per-kernel breakdown use CUPTI range tracing.
- Capture: nsight-sys --output=mytrace.qdrep --target-pid <pid> --duration=60s or run on containerized job with --trace=cupti.
- Convert to timeline and inspect memcpy stalls, kernel queuing, and streams concurrency.

eBPF and syscall tracing
- For I/O or epoll/syscall hotspots use bpftrace scripts (provided in tools/profiling). Common scripts: trace_epoll.bt, trace_sched.bt, tcp_latency.bt.
- Capture with sudo bpftrace trace_epoll.bt -o epoll.out and examine frequency of wakeups.

Perf CI job templates (example snip)
- The perf CI is defined in .github/workflows/perf.yml and in a Jenkins job for long-running benchmarks. The git-based CI should produce artifacts with consistent names. Example (YAML snippet):
  name: perf/regression
  on: [push]
  jobs:
    run-bench:
      runs-on: ubuntu-22.04
      steps:
        - uses: actions/checkout@v3
        - name: Build docker image
          run: docker build -t runtime-bench:${{ github.sha }} ./services/engine
        - name: Run synthetic workload
          run: docker run --rm --privileged runtime-bench:${{ github.sha }} /bin/bash -c "./bench/run.sh --model gpt-medium --batch 8 --duration 120"
        - name: Collect perf
          run: sudo perf record -F 120 -g -o /tmp/perf.data -- sleep 120
        - name: Upload artifacts
          run: aws s3 cp /tmp/perf.data s3://perf-artifacts/runtime/${{ github.sha }}/perf.data

Artifact checklist (what to collect)
- Flamegraph (SVG) and folded stacks (txt)
- perf.data and perf script output
- pprof.cpu and pprof.heap (if applicable)
- GPU trace (qdrep) and export to JSON/timeline
- Application logs (with correlation IDs) covering the collection window
- Node-level metrics (CPU, memory, disk, network, GPU utilization) and systemd/journald logs

How to analyze flamegraphs
- Look for tall stacks on the right (hot functions). Identify whether time is in user code, memcpy, syscalls, or runtime.
- Compare to baseline: overlay or diff folded stacks to see new or enlarged stacks.
- Common red flags: increased time in memcpy, epoll_wait wakeups, context-switch heavy functions, GC pauses (JVM), thread scheduling contention, or high serialization time in request handling.

Common bottlenecks and heuristics
- CPU-bound: High % in attention kernels, quantized dequantize/transpose ops, or token-output formatting. Check vectorized code paths and memory bandwidth.
- Memory bandwidth: High memcpy and cache-miss dominated stacks. Consider pinning NUMA, enabling hugepages, or reordering memory layout.
- GPU-bound: Long kernel queues, memcpy to/from device blocking kernels, or small kernels causing launch overhead. Use batching, overlap memcpy with compute, or use larger concurrencies.
- Lock contention: Look for lock/atomic hotspots in flamegraphs (mutex/condvar). Consider sharding data structures, lock-free queues.
- I/O: Blocking disk reads, metadata service calls, or slow KMS/HSM calls. Cache keys and use async I/O.

Debugging an example regression
1) Symptom: p99 latency increased from 220ms to 340ms after PR #2321.
2) Repro: Run bench with same prompts and batch config; confirm p99 increase locally.
3) Collect CPU flamegraphs before/after: found a new heavy stack in input preproc -> tokenize -> byte_decoder where time increased 5x due to an allocation-heavy change.
4) Mitigation: Revert tokenizer micro-change and file follow-up to optimize allocations.

Preserving and sharing artifacts
- Always attach perf artifacts to the Jira ticket. Include a short README with how the artifacts were collected and commands to reproduce.
- When sharing flamegraphs internally, point to the S3 URL and include commit, docker image, and runner node.
- For long investigations, create a docs/perf directory in the PR with reproduction scripts.

Automated alerts and triage rules
- Perf CI posts PR comments when a benchmark deviates >5% from baseline with links to artifacts. The comment includes a quick diff and the flamegraph link.
- If production-sampled telemetry shows p99 > SLA for 3 consecutive 5-min buckets, an incident is opened and on-call is paged. Attach sampled traces (1% sample) and the last successful benchmark.

Runbook checklist (step-by-step)
- Confirm workload and reproduce.
- Collect artifacts (flamegraph, pprof, gpu trace, logs).
- Upload and name artifacts correctly.
- Compare to baseline and identify top 3 hotspots.
- Short-term mitigation (rate limit, rollback) if production impact.
- File Jira with root cause hypothesis, artifacts, and next steps.

Appendix: useful commands (copy-paste)
- perf record: sudo perf record -F 99 -g -a -- sleep 60
- perf to folded: sudo perf script | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded
- flamegraph: ./flamegraph.pl out.folded > flame.svg
- pprof capture: curl -s localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=60 > cpu.prof
- async-profiler: ./profiler.sh -d 60 -f /tmp/profile.svg <pid>

Notes and open items
- Add an automated conversion from perf.data -> speedscope JSON in perf CI to ease interactive analysis (tracking: JIRA PERF-812).
- Validate async-profiler availability in production debug images.
- Add a standardized metadata.json for each artifact with fields: commit, docker_image, workload, duration, node_type.

If you're unfamiliar with any of the tools above, ping the eng-serving-runtime channel or @Riley Thompson for help.
